meta.title: Perfect Espresso at Home
meta.description: A systematic approach to dialing in espresso. Covers grind size, dose, yield, and timing for consistent shots every morning.

children.value: Espresso is not magic. It's a controlled extraction with four variables:
dose
(coffee in),
yield
(liquid out),
time
(how long), and
grind
(how fine). Change one, taste the result, adjust. That's the whole process.
Equipment You Actually Need
An espresso machine
— any machine with a 58mm portafilter and at least 9 bars of pressure. Entry-level: Breville Bambino. Mid-range: Lelit Anna.
A burr grinder
— this matters more than the machine. Blade grinders produce inconsistent particles that make dialing in impossible. Budget pick: 1Zpresso JX-Pro (hand) or Eureka Mignon Notte (electric).
A scale
— 0.1g resolution. You need to measure dose and yield precisely. Eyeballing is the enemy of consistency.
Fresh beans
— roasted within the last 3 weeks. Coffee degasses and goes stale. Supermarket beans are usually months old.
Do not buy a Nespresso machine and call it espresso. Pods produce coffee-flavored water at 2 bars of pressure. Real espresso requires 9 bars and freshly ground coffee. There is no shortcut.
The Recipe: A Starting Point
Start here and adjust to taste:

blocks.value:
Dose:    18g in
Yield:   36g out (1:2 ratio)
Time:    25-30 seconds
Temp:    93°C / 200°F

Adjust grind size to hit the time window.
Finer = slower. Coarser = faster.

children.value: Dialing In: A Step-by-Step Process

Grind 18g of coffee into the portafilter. Use a scale, not the grinder's timer — bean density varies. Distribute the grounds evenly with a WDT tool (a needle in a cork works fine) and tamp level with moderate pressure.
Place the cup on the scale, tare it, and start the shot. Watch the scale — you're targeting 36g of liquid. Stop the shot when you hit the target, and note the time.
Taste it. This is the most important step. Don't just look at numbers — your palate is the final judge.
Under-extracted. The water didn't pull enough flavor from the coffee. Fix: grind finer (slows the shot, increases extraction).
Over-extracted. Too much was pulled, including harsh compounds. Fix: grind coarser (speeds the shot, reduces extraction).
Sweet, complex, lingering finish. You've found the sweet spot. Write down your grind setting, dose, yield, and time. This is your recipe for this bag of beans.
Change
one variable at a time
. If the shot was sour, grind 1-2 clicks finer. If bitter, go coarser. Pull another shot and taste again. Most beans dial in within 3-4 shots.
Common Mistakes

Water finds the path of least resistance through the coffee puck. If there are gaps or uneven density, some areas over-extract while others under-extract. Symptoms: shot starts thin and watery, then suddenly gushes.
Fix: better distribution before tamping. Use a WDT tool to break up clumps. Tamp level — a crooked tamp creates a thin spot where water channels through.
Fresh-roasted beans need 5-7 days to degas before they're at peak espresso flavor. After 3-4 weeks, they've gone stale. The sweet spot is
7-21 days post-roast
Store beans in an airtight container at room temperature. Don't freeze them unless you're storing long-term — temperature cycling causes condensation inside the bag.

Single-boiler machines lose temperature when you pull a shot. Run a blank shot (no coffee) through the portafilter before your real shot to heat the group head and portafilter. This alone can fix sour, under-extracted espresso.
Espresso is a practice, not a recipe. The numbers are a starting point. Your palate is the instrument. Pull shots, taste, adjust, repeat.
